1. Site Preparation
.  Site clearing and preparatio n with installation of run-off 
control and excavation material containment measures to protect riparian zone 
and adjacent water-courses.

2. Caisson Installation .  Slip forming of a 4.9 m I.D. x 5.8 m O.D. reinforced 
concrete caisson to a depth of ± 30 m be low grade.  The caisson is cast on 
surface, with reinforcing as required, while the material below it is removed 
using a clam bucket.  As the subsoils  are removed and trucked offsite, the 
cast-and-cured concrete is allowed to slip into the excavation and concrete is 
cast on top to lengthen the casing as it is  sunk into position.  No dewatering is 
required for this part of the proce ss as the caisson, though formed and poured 
in the dry above ground surface, is inst alled in the wet below ground surface.  
The estimated time for this operation is 3.5 months.  The first caisson section 
lowered has up to 24 ports cast into it to allow subsequent installation of 
lateral casings and screens.  The total volume of soil to be removed during 
installation of the caisson is a bout 800 cubic metres.  The soil is 
uncontaminated mineral soil suitable for use as general grade fill.  Disposal 
location is not determined, but will not be  in riparian or aquatic environments, 
and appropriate measures will be ta ken to prevent sediment from soil 
placement from entering any riparian or aquatic environments.

3. Caisson Floor Installation .  Once the caisson reaches its design depth a 
concrete plug is poured through a tremie  pipe to the bottom of the casing to 
minimize contact between the water and the concrete, and allowed to cure.  
The caisson is then dewatered and clea ned and a permanent floor formed.  
Prior to the initial dewatering, the wate r quality in the caisson will be tested 
for pH and turbidity to confirm that it is suitable for discharge to the river.  If 
a suitable water quality is not achieved, the water will be discharged to a pit or 
playfield.

4. Installation of Lateral Well Screens
.  Lateral (horizontal) casings and well 
screens are projected at th e design depth (±29 m).  This process is similar to 
the installation of conventi onal vertical telescopic well screens:  Lateral well 
casings are hydraulically forced into th e formation at the design depth of the 
well screens.  Formation cuttings fall in to the casings via a slotted snout and 
are then washed back to the caisson.  The cuttings are s ubsequently removed 
to surface.  The casings are projecte d up to 46 m from the periphery of the 
caisson.  Slotted stainle ss steel well screens, sized to the formation 
encountered, are slid into the well casings and the well casings are withdrawn.  
Well screen is thus exposed to the adjacent formation.  During this process, 
the water flow from the well casings and screens is controlled, and is typically 
of the order of 10 litres per secon d, and often much less (Jack Brownell, 
International Water Supply Ltd., pers. comm, October 24, 2000).  Dewatering 
of the caisson is conducte d as required.  The water is normally clean and can 
be pumped from the bottom of the casing di rectly to the river.  If there is 
sediment resulting in excessive turbidity, the water would be pumped to a tank 
or settling basin before it is discharged  to the river.  The river discharge line 
will be constructed to minimize the poten tial for erosion and scour.  Up to 
24 lateral wells screens in three closely spaced lifts can be installed in the 
caisson size proposed.
5. Remove ancillary facilities as required.

Chemicals are stored in a limited access 
portion of the building accessible by authorized, trained personnel only.   
 
In treatment systems involving chlorine gas, there is an automatic alarm system which 
provides immediate notification of a chlori ne gas leak.  A blown safety plug in a 
pressurized chlorine tank is considered the worst possible accident with a chlorine 
treatment system.  City personnel are trained for dealing with chlorine leaks up and 
including a blown safety plug on a pressu rize tank.  The fire department also has 
personnel trained for such occurrences and ca rry the necessary equipment for addressing 
such problems on designated fire trucks.  Response would be by trained personnel 
following predetermined procedures.

5. Development of a contingency plan to address contamination incidents. 
 
It will also take into consideration the methods and protocols recommended in BC MELP 
(2000).

The City will monitor, report and evaluate e ffectiveness of the Wellhead Protection Plan 
on an annual basis by measuring water quality a nd water levels in a series of monitoring 
wells and/or piezometers installed as se ntinel wells to intercept any migrating 
contamination in sufficient time that it can be  identified, isolated and removed prior to 
having any influence on the collector well.  As  part of this Wellhead Protection Plan, the 
City will undertake measures to promote short and long term gr oundwater quality and 
prepare a plan to mitigate the impacts of any accident causing contamination of the 
aquifer.

Additional public cons ultation is planned during th e BCEAA Public Comment period, 
following acceptance of the City’s Application for a Project Approval Certificate by the 
Project Committee.  This will include publ ic notification and advertising of the 
Application submission.  The advertising will include notification of : 
 
• the EAO’s Project Registry web site where the Application can be viewed; 
• a designated location in the City of Kamloops where a copy of the document 
will be available for public view; and, 
• instructions on where and how to submit comments. 
 
At the public viewing location, the public wi ll be provided an opportunity to review the 
information provided, request City staff or  consultant (Golder) assistance, receive 
clarification on the project, and complete comment sheets.  
 
A Notification of the Application for a Projec t Approval Certificate will be published in 
the two local Kamloops newspapers ( Kamloops Daily News  and Kamloops This Week ) 
throughout the Public Comment Period, listing locations where the Application can be 
reviewed together with c ontact information (phone numbers, mailing addresses, and 
email addresses) for the City’s project st aff and their consultants (Golder) who can 
respond to enquiries.  The City will respond to  all inquires, either  in person or via 
telephone, facsimile, email, web page, or letter within 10 days of receipt of the same.

An Archaeological Impact Assessment was recently completed for the 
McArthur Island wellsite (Coates, 2000), with negative results .  No cultural 
material was observed on the ground surface in the area, or detected in shovel 
tests or deep test pits.  The stud y concluded that it is unlikely that 
undiscovered subsurface cultural materi als are present or would be impacted 
by the proposed development and recommended that no further 
archaeological work be conducted at the wellsite.  It is cautioned, however, 
that should archaeological remain s be encountered, all ground disturbance 
should immediately cease and the appropria te agencies contacted for further 
guidance.

5. Mr. John Jules indicated that a small nu mber (approximately 8) of Trumpeter 
Swans can often be found nesting and br eeding on McArthur Island and along 
the Thompson River shoreline, and s uggested that timing of construction 
should avoid sensitive nesting periods. 
 
The issue of nesting birds is recognized and will be addressed as described in 
Section 7.3.3.

The KIB has already identified issu es of importance to them in regard to this project, as 
described above.  The City recognizes the im portance of the views and concerns of the 
KIB regarding the proposed development and operation of the collector well, and will 
respond and address any additional issues th at may be identified by the First Nations 
community during the 30 day BCEAA public comment period following issuance of a 
Public Notice by the EAO.  The City will formally respond to any concerns and issues 
identified by the First Nations community, pr ior to the closure of the Public Comment 
Period.

5. Harmful Alteration, Disruption, or Dest ruction of Habitat (HADD) Associated 
with Construction of Ancillary Facilities across McArthur Island Slough 
 
Depending on construction method, it is possible that crossing of 
McArthur Island Slough for installation of water main and power supply line 
may result in HADD.  This will require determination of habitat losses, and 
creation of compensatory habitat consistent with the federal Policy for the 
Management of Fish Habitat.  DFO will then be requested to issue a Habitat 
Authorization Agreement under Section 35(2) of the federal Fisheries Act.

6. Navigable Waters Protection Act Approval 
 
Crossing of McArthur Island Slough may require an Approval under Section 5 
of the Navigable Waters Protection Ac t from the Canadian Coast Guard.  
Coast Guard has since responded to  indicate that Navigable Waters 
Protection Division approval is requi red for the slough crossings.  They have 
indicated that a 9.0 m clearance above high water, with appropriate marker 
spheres, is required for a temporary pow erline, but that 13 m clearance with 
marker spheres is required for a permanent powerline.

14. Wellhead protection Plan 
 
 The City will develop and implement a Wellhead Protection Plan.  The City 
will also consider existing and/or developing new municipal by-laws to 
regulate land use activities within the cap ture zone area.  Golder will provide 
technical and land use pla nning assistance to the City  w i t h  r e s p e c t  t o  t h e  
development and implementation of a Wellhead Protection Plan.
